headline: Help students build humanoid robots from the ground up.
lede: Metal2Humanoid is a proposed non-credit MIT IAP 2027 course in which about twenty students work in teams to build actuators, assemble them into a humanoid platform derived from Berkeley Humanoid Lite, and program it. The course requests no departmental funding: the organizing team is arranging hardware and materials through sponsors and parts donors, and the adapted design and course materials are released openly.

items.title: Reusable hardware
items.text: Actuator modules, limbs, and shared humanoid builds that are used across the four labs and kept for future offerings and community builds.

items.title: Prepared lab kits
items.text: Pre-fabricated and pre-sourced components, spares, and tools, so that 90-minute labs can focus on assembly, wiring, and testing rather than fabrication.

items.title: Documented learning resources
items.text: Lab guides, notebooks, and build notes published openly so that other groups can repeat the course.

needs.title: What we need
needs.intro: In-kind hardware is the most useful form of support: actuators and motors above all, then compute, printers and fabrication, tools and test equipment. Financial support covers what in-kind contributions do not, such as kit preparation, consumables, spares, and shipping.

items.title: Actuators, motors, encoders, and sensors
items.text: Joint actuators or motor-plus-gearbox modules, magnetic encoders, IMUs, and load sensing for the lab builds and spares.

items.title: Batteries, electronics, compute, and motor controllers
items.text: Battery packs and management, power distribution, motor controller boards, CAN interfaces, and on-board or bench compute.

items.title: Fabrication, machining, printing, and materials
items.text: 3D printing capacity and filament, laser-cut or machined interface parts, fasteners, bearings, and structural stock for kit preparation.

items.title: Tools, test equipment, spare parts, and consumables
items.text: Bench power supplies, multimeters, soldering stations, hand tools, robot support fixtures, cabling, and connectors.

items.title: Financial support
items.text: Funds for components, kit preparation, and replacement parts, used where in-kind contributions do not cover a need.

items.title: Technical mentorship and engineering support
items.text: Review of designs and lab procedures, help with motor control and firmware, and occasional guest participation in labs.

benefits.title: What sponsors receive
benefits.intro: We keep recognition straightforward and tied to real use of what you provide.
items: Recognition on this website and in relevant project materials.
Credited hardware demonstrations and build updates that show your components in use.
Opportunities to engage with student and independent robotics builders.
Practical feedback from hands-on use of your products in a teaching setting.
Participation in a growing open robotics education community.

bigCompanies.title: How Big Companies Fit In
bigCompanies.intro: Open robotics education and the companies that make robotics hardware need each other. The relationship works best when each side contributes what it is good at.

community.title: The community contributes
items: Experimentation with those technologies in real builds
Open documentation that others can follow
Honest, practical feedback from hands-on use
People who learn to build with those technologies

bigCompanies.partnerNote: For an actuator or motor manufacturer, the partnership can go further: the course platform and its open design can be built around your actuators, with published assembly guides, test data, and student builds that use them, and direct feedback from a cohort learning on your hardware. The v1 humanoid that follows the course build is not yet designed; we are waiting for sponsorship commitments before fixing it, so a hardware partner can shape it from the start.

noSponsorsNote: No sponsors are listed yet. Confirmed supporters will be recognized here with their permission.
facultyNote: Faculty sponsorship of the IAP proposal (Tomás Lozano-Pérez, MIT EECS) is an academic role and is separate from the financial and in-kind support described on this page.

contact.title: Get in touch
contact.text: Tell us what you can offer and any requirements your organization has for recognition, reporting, or shipping. We will reply with specifics about where it would be used.

whereItGoes.title: Where support goes
whereItGoes.intro: A small, non-credit course still needs real hardware. Here is what contributions are used for.
items: Actuator kits for every student: the Week 1 build, kept afterwards as reusable teaching modules.
Limb and lower-body assemblies for the team builds, plus one or two complete course robots and spares.
Compute for simulation and on-robot control, batteries, motor controllers, and sensors.
Kit preparation: printing, fasteners, bearings, cabling, test fixtures, and shipping between build sites.
Documentation and open release of the adapted design and the course materials.
